newsitem.title: UK: Aviation brokers brace for turbulent times.
newsitem.headline: Aviation brokers brace for turbulent times.

text.p: Aviation insurance brokers, already buffeted by a wave of industry consolidation, face serious additional challenges from clients and technological change.
Industry representatives told the 12th International Airline Insurance Conference that improved and expanded client service with fewer staff would be demanded of brokers over the next few years.
"The key is to make positive contributions to an airline's business rather than just being another bill to pay," Matthew Farrell, executive director of Willis Corroon Aerospace, told delegates.

In addition to arranging traditional hull and liability insurance cover, brokers will have to provide other services and help develop new products, including cover for currently uninsurable risks and total risk solutions.
"Brokers will have to help airlines tackle business risk issues as well as simple insurance issues," Farrell said.
David Binks, managing director of Alexander Howden Aviation Limited, a part of Aon, said brokers would also have to help airlines look for new risk transfer mechanisms.
Brokers will have to seek out alternatives to traditional insurance, such as futures and derivatives, for more demanding clients, Binks said.
"The role of the broker will continue to evolve. We will have to add more value to a transaction."
All this will have to be done with fewer staff and making greater use of new technology, such as that being offered by World Insurance Network (WIN), he added.

However, Farrell said he was optimistic about the future for brokers, noting that once the current spate of mergers and acquisitions has died down airline clients would want a wider choice than that offered by the few remaining mega-brokers.
Both Farrell and Binks believed that this would lead to the emergence of new, specialist brokers.
